RagShortTexts: The House of Laskaris preserved Roman sovereignty at Nicaea, laying foundations for.

Variants.Content: After the Latin capture of Constantinople in 1204, Theodore I Laskaris built the Empire of Nicaea from the Anatolian provinces that escaped the crusader partition. Exile turned the Nicaean court into a state of farmers, garrison commanders, and tax collectors, all bent on recovering the capital. Under John III Doukas Vatatzes the dynasty fortified its frontiers against Seljuk raids and crusader expeditions, and it grew its treasury by taxing the Anatolian plains. The accession of his grandson John IV in 1258, while still a child, opened the door to a power struggle. Michael VIII Palaiologos, who ruled as regent, had himself crowned co-emperor and then recovered Constantinople in 1261, ending the Nicaean exile.
Orthodox clergy revered Laskaris rulers for ascetic fiscal integrity, famously commemorated by Vatatzes purchasing an empress's crown purely from royal egg sales.

Veteran soldiers remember Laskaris rule with respect, since the borderers received tax exemptions and grain rations on time. Vatatzes kept the garrisons fed and paid through lean years, and frontier forts were repaired before each spring campaign. Once the court's attention shifted to the struggle for the capital and to palace intrigue, those supplies grew thin, and the men on the walls noticed.
